correctness.rationale: Musin Theorem 3.9 gives \(L_k(p,v_p(n))\le\varepsilon\) for every prime and \(\varepsilon\le U_k(q,v_q(n))\) for each \(q\mid n\). Because \(U_k(q,b)\) decreases in \(b\), \(q\mid n\) implies \(\varepsilon\le U_k(q,1)\); if \(p\nmid n\), then \(L_k(p,0)\le\varepsilon\). Hence \(L_k(p,0)>U_k(q,1)\) forces \(p\mid n\). Musin also proves every qualifying contact is even, so induction along certified adjacent-prime inequalities yields \(89\#\mid n\) at \(k=8\). The exact-rational verifier certifies all 23 strict inequalities and the reverse sign for \(89\to97\); it does not replace the universal induction.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Musin has the broadest directly relevant higher-order theory. Theorem 3.9 covers the same class of contacts, but its published consequence uses a coarse bound and gives only a one-shot sufficient order. Theorem 3.12 concerns asymptotic prime counts of successive first-contact quotients for a specific power-abscissa family, not a uniform order-8 support divisor over all Theorem-3.9 abscissas. Classical CA sources cover all classical maximizers but do not impose this higher-order level restriction.

value.rationale: Effective divisibility is a central arithmetic restriction developed in the motivating paper. The recursive lemma converts the paper's two-sided local bounds into a reusable forcing mechanism. Quantitatively, at order \(8\) the one-shot criterion directly certifies prime support only through \(5\), whereas the bootstrap certifies all \(24\) primes through \(89\), and it lowers the sufficient order for the natural divisor \(89\#\) from \(181\) to \(8\). The finite endpoint \(89\) is exact for this adjacent-prime method because the next comparison reverses.
